w: What's tested The blast rule: 20 percent blasts for most AML, and what blasts and Auer rods mean Acute versus chronic leukemia, and the two named ones: APL (bleeding, t(15;17), retinoic acid) and CML (the Philadelphia chromosome, imatinib) How lymphoma is diagnosed, the B symptoms, and Hodgkin versus the rest One defining feature of each lymphoma: its cell, its translocation or its infection What these diseases look like in the mouth Dr. Borak's lecture on Tuesday, November 17, covers the blood cancers: lymphomas, which start in the lymph system, and leukemias, which start in the marrow. These notes are from the slides; the lecture is Tuesday, and they will be checked against its recording. His objectives say you don't need the CD markers on his slides. How blood cells mature Every blood cell comes from a stem cell in the marrow, down a myeloid line (red cells, platelets, neutrophils, monocytes) or a lymphoid line (B, T and NK cells). A neutrophil grows up in this order: myeloblast, promyelocyte, myelocyte, metamyelocyte, band, segmented neutrophil. The blast is the youngest. What a lymphoma is A lymphoma is a cancer of lymphocytes that starts in the lymph system. You need a piece of tissue, a node or marrow, to diagnose it. The B symptoms A fever of 38 degrees Celsius or more with no cause, night sweats that soak the sheets, and losing at least 10 percent of your weight in 6 months without trying. The tissue and flow cytometry The lab looks at the cells (the H and E stain), stains the tissue with antibodies, and runs flow cytometry. Send the tissue for flow fresh, not in formalin, in a medium like RPMI or Hanks's solution, because flow needs living cells. Flow shines a laser through cells one at a time: forward scatter tells the size, side scatter tells how grainy the cell is. Classifying lymphoma It takes everything together, but how the cells look matters most. Most lymphomas, 85 to 90 percent, are B-cell. Most of the rest are T-cell; NK-cell ones are rare. Lymphoma near the mouth and eye Lymphoma can start in the eye (painless blurry vision or floaters), the tonsils, and the gums and lining of the mouth. Staging Staging asks how far it has spread: one node area, more than one on the same side of the diaphragm, both sides, or into organs like the marrow. B means B symptoms. What leukemia is Leukemia is cancer cells taking over the marrow and blood. It starts in the marrow and can spread to the spleen, liver and nodes. Untreated, it kills. It hurts you two ways. The marrow fails: anemia (tired, pale), low platelets (bruising, bleeding) and too few good white cells (fever, infections). And the cells move into organs: bone pain, a big spleen and liver, big nodes, nerve problems, and swollen gums. The marrow exam The back of the hip bone (posterior iliac crest) gives both a core biopsy and an aspirate. The sternum gives an aspirate only, and so does the tibia in small children. Acute versus chronic Acute: blasts, a fast start, death in under 6 months without treatment, low platelets, mildly enlarged organs. Chronic myeloid: mature cells, under 20 percent blasts, a slow start, 2 to 6 years without treatment, platelets normal or high at first, a big spleen. Both kill by infection or bleeding. AML and ALL AML is mostly in adults (median age 65). ALL is mostly in small children (peak at 2 to 3). Myeloblasts are bigger, with granules and sometimes Auer rods. Lymphoblasts are smaller, with little cytoplasm and no granules. An Auer rod means it isn't ALL. The number: most AML needs 20 percent blasts. If the AML has one of its defining genetic changes, the blast count doesn't matter. CLL/SLL Small, mature B cells in older people (median 70 or older). Called CLL when there are at least 5,000 per microliter of these B cells in the blood, SLL when it is mostly in the nodes. Same disease. On the smear: "soccer ball" chromatin and smudge cells. Infections come from low antibodies. It is slow but mostly incurable. Follicular lymphoma Crowded, back-to-back follicles. The translocation t(14;18) keeps BCL2 on, so the cells don't die. Usually widespread when found, but often without symptoms. Slow: median survival over 17 years. Mantle cell lymphoma From the mantle zone around the follicle. Small to medium cells with irregular nuclei, the translocation t(11;14), and a positive cyclin D1 stain. Older patients (median 68 to 69) with big nodes. Survival has gotten much better. MALT lymphoma A slow B-cell lymphoma outside the nodes, grown out of long inflammation. The stomach with H. pylori, the skin with Borrelia, the eye area with Chlamydia psittaci, the salivary gland after Sjögren syndrome, the thyroid after Hashimoto thyroiditis. Some respond to antibiotics. Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma Big B cells in sheets: about 30 percent of adult lymphomas. A node or mass that grows fast; 30 to 40 percent start outside the nodes (stomach, salivary glands, thyroid, bone). It can start on its own or grow out of a slow lymphoma. About 70 percent are doing well at 5 years after R-CHOP. Burkitt lymphoma Very fast-growing B cells. The translocation t(8;14) turns on MYC. Under the microscope: a starry sky, pale macrophages eating dead tumor cells among blue tumor cells. Endemic (equatorial Africa, Papua New Guinea): children, the jaws, EBV in over 90 percent. Sporadic (everywhere else): the abdomen, gums and tonsils, EBV in about 20 percent. Also seen with HIV. Jaw pain and loose teeth can be the first sign. Treatment works very well. Hodgkin lymphoma A few big Reed-Sternberg cells ("owl's eyes") in a crowd of normal immune cells. It stays in nodes above the diaphragm (the neck, above the collarbone, the chest) and spreads node to node in order. Painless, firm nodes; rarely, node pain after alcohol. Starting outside the nodes is rare. Nodular sclerosis has bands of scar tissue. EBV drives some cases. Over 80 percent are cured. The other lymphomas (non-Hodgkin) more often start outside the nodes and are more often widespread when found. Plasma cell tumors A plasmacytoma is one tumor of plasma cells. Multiple myeloma is plasma cells all through the marrow, making one antibody (the M-spike), with organ damage: CRAB, for high calcium, kidney damage, anemia and holes in the bones. Red cells stack like coins (rouleaux) because of all that antibody. Myeloma is usually incurable. T-cell lymphoma Peripheral T-cell lymphoma: adults, big nodes, B symptoms, aggressive. Mycosis fungoides and Sézary syndrome Mycosis fungoides: skin patches, then plaques, then tumors, often in the "bathing trunk" area; slow. Sézary syndrome: red skin all over, big nodes and the same cells (with brain-shaped nuclei) in the blood; aggressive. Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma It starts in the nose, destroys vessels and tissue, and can punch a hole in the hard palate. Strongly linked to EBV; mostly in eastern Asia and Indigenous peoples of Central and South America. CML The Philadelphia chromosome, t(9;22), makes BCR-ABL1, an enzyme stuck on. Most people are found in the slow chronic phase, sometimes by a routine blood count. The white count is very high (median about 80,000 per microliter), mostly neutrophils of every age, not blasts, and the spleen is big. Untreated, it turns into a blast phase in a few years. Imatinib (Gleevec) blocks the enzyme by taking ATP's place. Blasts and Auer rods Blasts mean acute leukemia, but a few (under 20 percent) can show up in MDS too. After the newborn period, any blast in the blood is abnormal. Auer rods are red-blue needles inside myeloblasts. APL A type of AML where the cells get stuck as promyelocytes, full of big granules and bundles of Auer rods. The translocation t(15;17) joins PML and RARA. The danger is DIC: bleeding gums, bruises, and early death. Retinoic acid with arsenic cures most. Acute monocytic leukemia An AML of monocyte-like cells with kidney-shaped nuclei. It can grow in the gums (myeloid sarcoma) and make them swell. Swollen gums in someone tired, pale and bruising: get a blood count. B-ALL and T-ALL B-ALL is the most common leukemia in children (75 percent are under 6), with a smaller second peak in the 40s. It shows as marrow failure. Over 90 percent of children do well. T-ALL looks the same under the microscope; it often has a high white count and a mass in the chest, and the lymphoma form can block the airway. Where acute leukemia comes from It can be the end of another marrow disease (MDS, CML, CMML, or a myeloproliferative neoplasm: polycythemia vera with too many red cells, essential thrombocythemia with too many platelets, myelofibrosis with a scarred marrow). It can come within 10 years of chemotherapy or radiation for another cancer, with a bad prognosis. And it can come with Down syndrome. Treatment Kill the leukemia (chemotherapy, radiation, transplant) and support the patient. The goal is complete remission: no symptoms, no disease found, normal blood counts. The translocations t(14;18), BCL2 Follicular lymphoma t(11;14), cyclin D1 Mantle cell lymphoma t(8;14), MYC Burkitt lymphoma t(9;22), BCR-ABL1 (Philadelphia) CML t(15;17), PML-RARA APL In the mouth Swollen gums: AML in the gums. Bleeding gums and spots: low platelets, or DIC in APL. A fast jaw mass in a child: Burkitt. A hole in the palate: NK/T-cell lymphoma. A new parotid lump with Sjögren: MALT lymphoma. Punched-out holes in the jaw with high calcium: myeloma.
